comments.text:
@WesRoth, in your video and others there has been a highlight of the energy production by China compared to the US.  Important as it is 'in the long term', a more refined analysis tells a very different story.  Energy production is a critical factor in the AI race between the US and China.  One measure of production is simply GW produced.  However, this simplistic metric ignores other factors such as population size.  Perhaps a more refined metric of energy production is GDP/GW.
The GDP/GW metric is significant because it measures how efficiently a country generates economic output per unit of energy produced, accounting for differences in population and economic scale. It reflects energy utilization in driving economic activity, crucial for AI development, which demands high computational power and energy.
Here's a comparison based upon 2023 data:
US: GDP ~$29.2 trillion, electricity capacity ~1,200 GW. GDP/GW ~$24.3 million/GW.
China: GDP ~$17.8 trillion, electricity capacity ~2,920 GW. GDP/GW ~$6.1 million/GW.
In other words, the US is roughly 4x more efficient in generating GDP per GW.  The more energy-efficient economy is due to advanced technology and higher-value industries in the US. China, with a larger population and industrial focus, produces more total GW but less GDP per unit, which reflects its higher energy use for manufacturing (often times of low-tech commodity goods). For AI, the US's efficiency edge supports scaling compute-intensive tasks with less energy infrastructure, although China's raw capacity could drive significant AI resources if the country were able to redirect its economic focus away from manufacturing.
